Where it began

Rishabh Pant was born in Haridwar, Uttarakhand, on 4 October 1997. At 12 he began making weekend trips to Delhi to train under Tarak Sinha at the Sonnet academy, and his coach asked him to rebuild his batting from the ground up. The moment it clicked, by his own account, was a Delhi Under-19 match against Assam, when he followed 35 in the first innings with 150 in the second.

He was vice-captain of India at the 2016 Under-19 World Cup, where he hit a fifty from 18 balls against Nepal, at the time the fastest at that level. Back home he made 308 in a Ranji Trophy innings against Maharashtra and, against Jharkhand, a hundred from 48 balls, the quickest the competition had seen.

The player

His Test debut came against England in August 2018, and he got off the mark with a six, the first Indian to start that way. Within a month he made his first Test hundred, becoming the first Indian wicketkeeper to reach three figures in a Test in England, and in January 2019 he did the same in Australia. Behind the stumps he held eleven catches in the first Test of that tour, more than any Indian keeper had managed in a Test.

By October 2026 he had played 52 Tests and made 3,725 runs at 43.82, with eight hundreds, 21 fifties and a best of 159 not out, as well as 166 catches and 18 stumpings. At Headingley in June 2025 he made a hundred in each innings, the first Indian to do so in a Test in England and only the second wicketkeeper anywhere after Andy Flower.

What made him special

He played the game as if the scoreboard owed him something. The innings people remember came at Brisbane in January 2021, where Australia had not lost a Test there since 1988: India were set 328 in the fourth innings, and his unbeaten 89 on the final day took them home. A few days earlier at Sydney he had made 97 from 118 balls when the job was simply to survive. In 2022 he reached fifty against Sri Lanka in 28 balls, then the fastest by an Indian in a Test, and he went on to become the fourth batter to hit 100 Test sixes.

There were quieter spells, too, and for a while he had to bat in the long shadow of MS Dhoni. He answered in the best way, with runs.

Away from the middle

He was named the ICC's Emerging Cricketer of the Year for 2018 and, in February 2021, became the first winner of its Player of the Month award. After more than a year away from the game, he came back in 2024 and played his part in India's T20 World Cup win that June, and in 2025 he added the Champions Trophy. That return earned him a nomination for the Laureus Comeback of the Year award in 2025.

And finally

Most batters like to get off the mark with a quiet single. Pant chose to clear the rope, and Test cricket was rarely quiet with him in it.
